newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian farmers claim support on native rights.
newsitem.headline: Australian farmers claim support on native rights.

text.p: Australia's top farming group said on Tuesday that almost two in three people supported its push for farmers to be protected against Aboriginal land claims.

The National Farmers' Federation said polling conducted in response to a television advertising campaign on land rights found 62 percent of those surveyed backed the farmers and 58 percent believed their plight was genuine or believable.

Farmers are pressing the national government to legislate to give pastoral leases -- leasers granted to farmers and graziers since white settlement began more than 200 years ago -- supremacy over Aboriginal land rights claims.

"Obviously, our message -- for the restoration of the rights of farmers -- cut through the 'media clutter' and was accepted by our target audience," federation executive director Wendy Craik said in a speech.

The conservative Liberal-National government is due soon to announce its response to a December High Court ruling, known as the Wik decision, that pastoral leases did not automatically wipe out "native title".
Farm groups say the Wik ruling created uncertainty about what they can do with their land and jeopardised rural industry.

The uncertainty extends to mining and exploration on pastoral land. Queensland said last month it had frozen about 500 mining exploration applications until the issue of land tenure security was settled.
Senior ministers were discussing their options at a regular cabinet meeting on Tuesday.
Prime Minister John Howard said no decision has been made, but he pledged t0 look after farmers and the rural industry, worth an estimated A$34 billion (US$27 billion) a year.
"I can certainly assure them that I am not going to sell them short, I'm not going to sell them out and I'm not going to let them down," he said.
Howard said he was still seeking a compromise deal between farmers and Aborigines, but was prepared to impose a solution if no agreement could be struck.
Native title rights were granted to Aborigines three years ago by the former Labor government but the relationship between Aboriginal claims and pastoral leases was left ill-defined.

Already more than a third of Australian land is being claimed by indigenous Aborigines and the premier of the northern state of Queensland, the National Party's Rob Borbidge, has said 85 percent of the state could be hit by claims.

The farmers' federation ran a series of television advertisements targeted at city people to win support for their cause. The ads aroused Aboriginal anger because they featured white and black children playing complicated games -- which the black child always won.
